brief.head: Advanced, persistent
brief.text: Attacks that are both skilled and sus­tained point to a state, Ajay Shah said. Private crim­i­nals “launch one crime and then they’ll lose in­ter­est”. {084-C04}

brief.head: Fight it anyway
brief.text: Most mis­in­for­ma­tion is home­grown, Amit Varma guessed. Since at­tri­bu­tion is hard, fight it wher­ever it comes from: China, Russia or “some guy sit­ting in UP”. {084-C13}

brief.head: Debugged in India
brief.text: Global at­tack groups test their new­est zero-day ex­ploits on Indian tar­gets, Ajay Shah said, be­cause breaches here get hushed up. A week later, they hit Europe and America. {084-C12}

brief.head: Sincere, not bought
brief.text: Most pro-Russian views in America are sin­cerely held, Amit Varma said. Calling them for­eign-sponsored is like the Indian gov­ern­ment brand­ing dis­si­dents “anti-national”[[x4]]. {084-C14}

brief.head: Lawyers for the CIA
brief.text: Authoritarian states launch dirty tricks eas­ily, Ajay Shah said, free of leg­is­la­tures and in­for­ma­tion laws. The CIA, by con­trast, has to con­sult lawyers at every step. {084-C05}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on hybrid warfare
lead.head: Not quite war, not quite peace

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 84

body: Amit Varma began by declar­ing that he and Ajay Shah are men of peace. They then spent nearly an hour and a half on war, of a kind that often does not look like war at all.
There used to be a sim­ple choice, Shah said: a coun­try was ei­ther at peace or at war. Now the world is shaded grey.

At one ex­treme is ex­plicit war, as be­tween Russia and Ukraine. At the other is ex­plicit peace, as be­tween Japan and the United States. In the mid­dle lies a grey zone of hos­tile acts. That is the zone of hy­brid war[[x1]].
## Below the thresh­old

The field’s terms are de­tec­tion, at­tri­bu­tion and re­sponse. The ideal at­tack is one the vic­tim never no­tices; the next best, one it can­not pin on any­one. Either way, hit­ting back be­comes hard.
“Show me a hos­tile ac­tion that can stay below the at­tri­bu­tion thresh­old,” Shah said. “Okay, that’s the game.” {084-C01}
There is a catch, and it is time. Detection and at­tri­bu­tion usu­ally ar­rive in the end, so the at­tacker who plays short gets a punch in now and the bill later.

Shah’s tool­kit has four draw­ers: cyber at­tacks routed through friendly countries’ IP ad­dresses; prox­ies such as the Wagner group and Lashkar-e-Taiba; in­for­ma­tion war­fare, newly po­tent on so­cial media; and de­ni­able vi­o­lence, such as a tanker’s an­chor dragged across the Baltic seabed. {084-C03}
## Cheap shots
Hybrid war­fare, Shah ar­gued, is the strat­egy of the weak. Putin, “a very weak player” hold­ing a GDP he put at the size of Italy’s, gets out­sized re­turns from cheap op­er­a­tions.
Every small at­tack car­ries a veiled threat of big­ger ones, he said, and the fear it breeds strength­ens those in the tar­get coun­try who want to make peace.

Yet he would not call it a win­ning strat­egy. Pakistan’s hawks might score the 2008 Mumbai at­tack a suc­cess, but the coun­try paid with iso­la­tion. It suits, he said, those “man­ag­ing the head­lines and not the coun­try”.

Varma pushed back on how much could be pinned on for­eign plots. India’s Hindu-Muslim ten­sions are home­grown, he said. Shah agreed: in­for­ma­tion war­fare can­not in­vent a society’s fault lines, only in­flame the ones it finds.
## Wake-up call

The most dan­ger­ous idea, Shah said, is that all this hap­pens else­where, in the Baltic or in Australian elec­tions. By one es­ti­mate, about 43 per cent of Russia’s in­flu­ence cam­paign on the Ukraine war was con­ducted in India. {#fortythree}
India should not read the for­eign press and con­clude that it is safe, he said. It is al­ready part of the global game.

His reme­dies ran from a faster armed re­sponse to ter­ror to bet­ter gov­ern­ment soft­ware. Against in­for­ma­tion war­fare, he ar­gued, the only real de­fence is a society’s abil­ity to es­tab­lish what is true: uni­ver­si­ties, sta­tis­tics, re­searchers, trusted media and be­liev­able gov­ern­ment bod­ies. {084-C15}
Fact-checkers, Shah said, are “but a thin layer on a deeper so­ci­etal ca­pa­bil­ity”. And “it is dif­fi­cult and dan­ger­ous to be a truth teller in India today”.

Varma ended with a con­fes­sion. Every time he vis­its Shah’s home, he said, he is plied with fruit, biryani and sweets: hy­brid war­fare, he now re­alised. “You’re killing me softly with your sugar.” {084-J06}

second.label: The Baltic Sea
second.head: Oops, said the tanker
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a Chinese tanker, a torn seabed and a Finnish boarding party

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Baltic anchor drag

body: Russia runs a “shadow fleet” of tankers that carry its crude oil to friendly buy­ers[[x2]], China and India among them. A Chinese tanker in that fleet, Ajay Shah said, dragged its an­chor along the floor of the Baltic Sea, tear­ing through gas pipe­lines, oil pipe­lines and fibre-optic lines. {084-S02}

Even when caught, such a crew can call it an ac­ci­dent. This time the Finnish Navy boarded the ship and de­tained the crew for in­ter­ro­ga­tion. Shah likened it to India tak­ing Kasab alive in 2008, and called the in­ci­dent an un­prece­dented es­ca­la­tion.
Amit Varma imag­ined the board­ing party’s reply to the cap­tain: “We are Finnish, you are fin­ished.” {084-J02}

quote.text: The tanker throws up its hands and says, oops, this was a mis­take.

third.head: Centrifuges in a spin

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the code in Iran’s centrifuges

body: The Israelis, long keen to dis­rupt Iran’s nu­clear pro­gramme[[x3]], got into the op­er­at­ing sys­tem of the in­dus­trial con­trollers that ran Iran’s cen­trifuges, Ajay Shah said. {084-S01}

The code knew the fre­quen­cies the ma­chines needed. Whenever sci­en­tists asked a cen­trifuge to do the right thing, it made the cen­trifuge do the wrong thing. Machines fell apart, and the ura­nium pu­rifi­ca­tion went wrong.
“For a long time the sci­en­tists thought that we have not yet solved our R and D prob­lems,” Shah said, “while ac­tu­ally there was clever code that was dis­rupt­ing them.”

Even after the sab­o­tage was found, Iran was left ask­ing who did it and how to re­spond. That, Shah said, is the craft of hy­brid war­fare: stay­ing below the thresh­olds of de­tec­tion and at­tri­bu­tion. {084-C01}

p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s map of hybrid warfare, part by part, and where Amit Varma pushed back

from1.head: Not quite war, not quite peace

quote.text: So peo­ple have ap­plied them­selves to say­ing what things can I do to harm my en­e­mies with­out get­ting to de­tec­tion or at­tri­bu­tion.

box.title: Detect, attribute, respond
box.text: Detection: does the vic­tim even know it was at­tacked? Attribution: can it tell who did it? Response: can it hit back? Hybrid war­fare, Ajay Shah said, is the craft of stay­ing below the first two thresh­olds. {084-C01}

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: Four tools, no fingerprints
sections.caption: the hybrid toolkit
body: Imagine India’s elec­tric­ity grid mis­be­hav­ing: fre­quen­cies going wrong, equip­ment dam­aged, and no­body know­ing why. That, Ajay Shah said, is a cyber at­tack still below the de­tec­tion thresh­old. {084-C03}

Attribution is no eas­ier. Attackers first log in through a friendly coun­try, so hun­dreds of IP ad­dresses from Japan may seem to be at­tack­ing Indian power sys­tems. Investigators must study the code it­self, its DNA and an­tecedents, and work out which mod­i­fi­ca­tion hap­pened where.
Russia and China, he said, also grew pri­vate cyber gangs[[x5]] on pur­pose. Caught out, a gov­ern­ment can apol­o­gise for “some crim­i­nals” and offer to jail them.
## Proxies and pro­pa­ganda

Proxies serve the same end. Wagner let Russia call its fight­ers mer­ce­nar­ies, and Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed let Pakistan’s gov­ern­ment plead “Who me?”. In Donetsk, many local “rebels” were Russian sol­diers in guer­rilla uni­forms.

Propaganda is old, Shah said: the Soviet Union did it, and the West had Voice of America. What is new is so­cial media, whose rab­bit holes rad­i­calise and trib­alise. He de­scribed blow-by-blow ev­i­dence that Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Internet Research Agency in St Petersburg stoked American anger all the way to a phys­i­cal rally in Colorado. {084-S10}
~ Amit Varma ac­cepted that Russia had tried to in­ter­fere in the 2016 elec­tion, but said its ef­fect was vastly over­stated and had no im­pact on the re­sult. {#overstated}

quote.text: So peo­ple have ap­plied them­selves to say­ing what things can I do to harm my en­e­mies with­out get­ting to de­tec­tion or at­tri­bu­tion.

sections.label: The incentives
sections.head: The weakling’s weapon
sections.caption: the strategy of the weak
body: Hybrid war­fare is cho­sen be­cause it is op­ti­mal for some peo­ple, Ajay Shah said. They are “play­ing their chess game as well as they can”, and it is the strat­egy of the weak. {084-C02}

Russia, he said, is be­lieved to have tested the idea on Paris: some four­teen fibre-optic ca­bles into the city were cut at once, by peo­ple who un­der­stood the whole net­work. It was a nui­sance in peace­time. The un­stated mes­sage was that the same might be done to twenty European cities. {084-S03}
Such fear feeds the peace­mak­ers. Germany’s long soft­ness on Putin, Shah ar­gued, was born of it. Influence op­er­a­tions, he added, are “all very low cost af­fairs”.
## Late is too late

Deniability need not last for­ever. In Crimea, Putin’s men in plain clothes, nick­named the Little Green Men, claimed to be a local mili­tia. The Obama team was fooled for a while, and by the time it un­der­stood, the Russian army con­trolled Crimea. {084-S04}

Democracies are ex­posed in an­other way[[x6]]. Divide a coun­try against it­self, Shah said, and it can­not mount an ef­fec­tive for­eign pol­icy. {084-C07} He called the rise of pro-Russian views in American pol­i­tics one of Putin’s great­est achieve­ments.
~ Amit Varma replied that Putin in­vaded no one in Trump’s first term.

quote.text: Hiding in­side every small at­tack is a veiled threat about big­ger at­tacks in the fu­ture.

sections.label: The pushback
sections.head: Don’t read history backwards
sections.caption: the hindsight teleology trap
body: Five peo­ple in­side Pakistan’s ISI, Ajay Shah said, could write a one-sided re­port card on the 2008 Mumbai at­tack and high-five all round. But the coun­try paid with iso­la­tion as Fortune 500 boards backed away. Such tac­tics suit those whose “de­ci­sion hori­zon is one week”. {084-C09}

Amit Varma pushed back on the ex­am­ples. The com­mu­nal strain has run through Indian so­ci­ety all along, he said, as Akshaya Mukul’s his­tory of the Gita Press shows. Foreign pow­ers might act at the mar­gins. {084-R03}

Nor could any­one have planned what fol­lowed 26/11. The economy’s slide after P. Chidambaram was moved from the fi­nance min­istry[[x7]], de­scribed in Puja Mehra’s *The Lost Decade*[[x8]], was be­yond any plot­ter. Reading such chains back­wards is, Varma said, the “hind­sight tele­o­log­i­cal mis­take”. {084-C08}
## Fires, not matches

Shah agreed. The prob­lems are home­grown, he said, but in­for­ma­tion war­fare finds a country’s weak spots and plays on them. Karl Popper, he noted, warned against com­plex con­spir­acy the­o­ries: no­body can plan so much, “least of all a se­cret small cabal of con­spir­a­tors”. {084-J14}
Varma also de­fended the mar­ket­place of ideas: most pro-Russian views in America, he ar­gued, are sin­cere, not bought.
~ Shah’s own ex­am­ple of un­in­tended con­se­quences: who could have pre­dicted that the October 7 at­tack would lead to the fall of the Assad regime?

quote.text: It is deeply to­tal­i­tar­ian to say that my view is right, and any other view is some for­eign agents are doing it.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the hindsight teleology trap

sections.label: The spy game
sections.head: Spies, lies and timing
sections.caption: intelligence, early and deep
body: Early de­tec­tion and at­tri­bu­tion are key against in­for­ma­tion war­fare, Ajay Shah said. Once a cam­paign is ex­posed, peo­ple dis­count it, be­cause “the peo­ple are rea­son­ably bright”. {084-C10}

Amit Varma raised the hard part. Every in­tel­li­gence agency, in­clud­ing France’s, be­lieved Iraq had weapons of mass de­struc­tion, and all of them were wrong. In a sea of noise, how does any­one know what to trust?

Shah an­swered with three sto­ries. In Iraq, Western agen­cies trusted doc­u­ments writ­ten by of­fi­cials too fright­ened to re­port fail­ure. In Crimea, they worked out too late what was hap­pen­ing.
## The one that worked

The third was a tri­umph. In February 2022, be­fore Russia in­vaded Ukraine, the Biden team pub­lished its in­tel­li­gence: the plan, the dates, which tank would move where. Nobody could then pass the in­va­sion off as a local up­ris­ing. {084-S05}

Varma asked about pri­vate ac­tors, from a bil­lion­aire short­ing stocks to “some kid in a pa­jama in a bed­room”. Shah of­fered a term of art: APT, or ad­vanced per­sis­tent threat. Teenage hack­ers are rarely ad­vanced, and crim­i­nals rarely per­sist. Only states are both. {084-C04}
~ The foot­print of in­tel­li­gence, Shah said, must widen be­yond tra­di­tional war to every piece of hy­brid war­fare, though mis­takes will al­ways be made.

quote.text: But if a cam­paign is de­tected early and the at­tri­bu­tion is done early, then ac­tu­ally the peo­ple are rea­son­ably bright.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: The battlefield at home
sections.caption: India as a battlefield
body: The most dan­ger­ous thing, Ajay Shah said, is to read about the Baltic Sea or Australian elec­tions and as­sume noth­ing is hap­pen­ing in India. His XKDR Forum has a work­ing paper gath­er­ing ev­i­dence on for­eign ac­tors around Indian elec­tions. {084-R02}

In 2021, he said, Meta doc­u­mented a Russian in­flu­ence op­er­a­tion in India against the AstraZeneca vac­cine. Developed with Oxford and made at scale by the Serum Institute with help from the Gates Foundation, it had helped the sub­con­ti­nent fight COVID. Russia did not want that good­will going to the West. {084-S11}
Amit Varma had three shots of it, and was glad. Without the vac­cine, he told Shah, “You could have been talk­ing to an empty chair.” Shah’s reply: “Everything is noth­ing.” {084-J05}
## Records of the pow­er­ful

Attacks on India’s power sys­tem in 2022 are be­lieved to have come from China, Shah said. So is the hack of AIIMS, which stole the med­i­cal records of pow­er­ful Indians, “a gold mine” for fu­ture covert op­er­a­tions.
~ It is time to wake up, he said, though not to start shout­ing “for­eign hand” at every dis­si­dent.

quote.text: Because they did not want Indian good­will in favor of Oxford University and AstraZeneca, a Western Corporation, and the Gates Foundation.

sections.label: The remedies
sections.head: Guns faster, truth deeper
sections.caption: the defences that work
body: Each threat needs its own an­swer, Ajay Shah said. Against prox­ies and ter­ror, build ki­netic ca­pa­bil­ity: when the next at­tack comes at the Taj, “get guns there faster”.

Against cyber at­tacks, build bet­ter sys­tems. India calls it­self an IT su­per­power, yet global at­tack groups use it as a train­ing ground, he said: mis­con­fig­ured sys­tems abound, and com­pa­nies hush up breaches rather than alert ven­dors. New zero-day at­tacks are de­bugged on Indian tar­gets, then taken to Europe and America a week later. {084-C12}
## Truth as a de­fence

Information war­fare de­mands some­thing deeper. Every so­ci­ety, Shah said, needs epis­temic in­sti­tu­tions to sep­a­rate truth from lies: uni­ver­si­ties, sta­tis­tics, re­searchers, trusted media and gov­ern­ment bod­ies that peo­ple be­lieve. {084-C15}
Where those in­sti­tu­tions are weak, as he said they are in India, ma­nip­u­la­tors do­mes­tic and for­eign have a field day.

Amit Varma ex­plained to lis­ten­ers that epis­temic means knowl­edge. He had ear­lier ar­gued that mis­in­for­ma­tion should be fought wher­ever it comes from, guess­ing that ninety per cent of it is lo­cally gen­er­ated. {#ninety}
~ The United States came through Cold War pro­pa­ganda, Shah said, be­cause trusted peo­ple spoke up, wrote and crit­i­cised, and were be­lieved.

quote.text: The only way to fight in­for­ma­tion war is to grow the depth and ca­pa­bil­ity and ac­tivism of that epis­temic in­sti­tu­tional ca­pa­bil­ity.
The prob­lems are home­grown. But it is the na­ture of in­for­ma­tion war­fare that you will iden­tify the dif­fi­cul­ties of the coun­try and pour oxy­gen on the fires.

p3.title: Dispatches from the shadows
p3.deck: A loudspeaker duel, a brave constable, phantom weapons and a buggy study

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a propaganda war at Nathu La, 1967
stories.head: Loud, clear and incomprehensible
body: In 1965, Amit Varma said, the Indian Army ex­pected China to push into Sikkim through two passes, Jelep La and Nathu La. It or­dered a pull­back, so they could be de­fended from wider po­si­tions. The gen­eral at Jelep La with­drew. Sagat Singh, at Nathu La, re­fused[[x9]]. {084-S08}

Singh’s think­ing, as Varma put it: “What if they just want to oc­cupy?” High ground lets a few men de­fend against many below. The puz­zled Chinese held off, and when fight­ing came in 1967, at Nathu La and Cho La, they were re­pelled.

It was at Nathu La, Varma said, draw­ing on Probal Dasgupta’s *Watershed 1967*, that the Chinese army tried pro­pa­ganda. It trans­lated its mes­sages into Shuddh Hindi and played them to the Indian sol­diers over loud­speak­ers. {084-S09}

“Now, as you and I and every Indian knows, no one in India speaks Shuddh Hindi[[x10]],” Varma said. It is an ar­ti­fi­cial reg­is­ter, born of a 19th-century move­ment to split Hindustani. And the sol­diers were Jats, who had no idea what was being said.
Assuming the broad­casts were work­ing, the Chinese went from four loud­speak­ers to twelve. {#loudspeakers}

The Indians, bizarrely, had loud­speak­ers of their own, and shouted pro­pa­ganda back in Chinese. Ajay Shah asked lis­ten­ers to spare a thought for those sol­diers, work­ing “pre-Google Translate”. {084-J03}

~ Whether India’s Chinese slo­gans worked, no­body on this side knows. “It’s al­most like a comic book thing,” Varma said. Even then, armies un­der­stood that in­for­ma­tion can take morale up or down.
stories.why: Information has al­ways been a weapon of morale, but it works only on an au­di­ence that un­der­stands it. Get the lan­guage wrong and you can scale up a use­less op­er­a­tion with com­plete con­fi­dence.
stories.postscript: Varma ar­gued that a Chinese hold on Nathu La could have cut India off from East Pakistan in the 1971 war.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Nathu La loudspeakers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a constable’s sacrifice in 2008
stories.head: The man who would not let go
body: During the 2008 at­tack on Mumbai, Amit Varma said, the con­sta­ble Tukaram Omble was on Marine Drive when Ajmal Kasab, one of the at­tack­ers, tried to get away.
Omble grap­pled and fought with him, and held on so that Kasab could be taken alive. He was shot in the process and died. {084-S06}

Because Kasab sur­vived, India could learn where he was born and trained, and show that this was proxy war­fare by Pakistan. “Had all the men died,” Varma said, “they had com­plete plau­si­ble de­ni­a­bil­ity.” {#deniability}
~ Varma ac­cused Ajay Shah of hav­ing stolen this talk­ing point ear­lier, when Shah ex­plained why the Finnish Navy’s board­ing of a Chinese tanker in the Baltic mat­tered so much.
stories.why: In de­ni­able war­fare, at­tri­bu­tion can hang on a sin­gle thread. One constable’s grip turned an anony­mous strike into a doc­u­mented, state-backed op­er­a­tion. Varma called him one of India’s great he­roes.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why every intelligence agency got Iraq wrong
stories.head: The weapons that lived on paper
body: Every in­tel­li­gence agency, Amit Varma noted, even that of France, which op­posed the in­va­sion of Iraq, be­lieved Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass de­struc­tion. Ajay Shah ex­plained what went wrong.

Under a tyrant who would de­stroy any­one re­port­ing fail­ure, Iraqi civil ser­vants wrote that they were mak­ing great progress. Their bi­o­log­i­cal weapons, the files said, were killing mice; mon­keys were next. {084-S12}
Those doc­u­ments leaked to Western agen­cies, which be­lieved the hard paper. Saddam re­fused in­spec­tions, and only when an army went in did any­one find the labs empty.

~ “It is Swachh Bharat all over again[[x11]],” Shah said: non­sense flows up a bu­reau­cracy until the top be­lieves it. A doc­u­ment say­ing so many toi­lets were built, he warned, is no rea­son to start cheer­ing. {084-J13}

quote.text: In Saddam Hussein’s regime, you needed to have that so­ci­o­log­i­cal un­der­stand­ing of the Saddam regime, that of­fi­cials lie to each other.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on fake reports from Saddam’s Iraq

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s “world’s best story”, for researchers
stories.head: A bug in the conspiracy
body: Ajay Shah billed it as the world’s best story, for re­searchers. Amit Varma said he was “so ex­cited now”, since that sounded like his own habit. {084-J04}

Shortly after the October 7 at­tack, Shah said, a re­search paper in America claimed some­one had taken a vast short po­si­tion on Israeli mar­kets just be­fore it. The plot­ters, it im­plied, had made half a bil­lion dol­lars off their own atroc­ity. {#shortbet}
Then came the punch­line. “It turned out that there were mis­takes in the pro­gram­ming,” Shah said, “so the re­sult was ac­tu­ally wrong.” {084-S13}
~ Varma, for his part, had al­ready said that the sheer evil of the at­tack dwarfed any trad­ing profit: “You’re killing eleven hun­dred peo­ple or you’re short­ing some­thing?”
stories.why: Terror and profit can mix in prin­ci­ple, which makes at­tri­bu­tion harder still. But a sen­sa­tional find­ing de­serves sus­pi­cion until its code has been checked, a les­son Shah aimed squarely at re­searchers.

quiz.q: What nickname was given to the plain-clothes men who took over Crimea?
quiz.a: The Little Green Men, who claimed to be a local mili­tia, not Russian sol­diers.

quiz.q: What does APT stand for, and why does it usually point to a state?
quiz.a: Advanced per­sis­tent threat; only states buy such skill and keep at it.

quiz.q: Which constable held Ajmal Kasab on Marine Drive so he could be taken alive?
quiz.a: Tukaram Omble, who was shot and killed keep­ing Kasab from es­cap­ing.

quiz.q: Why did the Chinese loudspeaker propaganda at Nathu La fail with the Jat soldiers?
quiz.a: It was in Shuddh Hindi, an ar­ti­fi­cial reg­is­ter that no­body in India speaks.

quiz.q: What did the Biden team do with its intelligence before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022?
quiz.a: It made it pub­lic: the in­va­sion plan, the dates, which tanks would move where.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did Western agencies believe Iraq had weapons of mass destruction?
quiz.a: Frightened Iraqi of­fi­cials faked progress re­ports, and leaked doc­u­ments were taken at face value.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 84. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Karl Popper (Franz Barta, No restrictions); Vladimir Putin (Пресс-служба Президента России, CC BY 4.0); Yevgeny Prigozhin (Михаил Метцель / ТАСС, CC BY 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Watershed 1967: India’s Forgotten Victory Over China
shelf.creator: Probal Dasgupta
shelf.why: It tells the lit­tle-known story of India push­ing China back in 1967.

shelf.title: Concerns About Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI): An Indian Perspective
shelf.creator: University of Navarra and XKDR Forum
shelf.why: It col­lects global ev­i­dence and frag­ments of hard in­for­ma­tion about for­eign ac­tors around Indian elec­tions.

shelf.title: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
shelf.creator: Akshaya Mukul
shelf.why: Mukul’s mas­ter­piece shows how deeply Hindu na­tion­al­ist ideas ran through Indian so­ci­ety over the decades: the com­mu­nal strain was there all along, sec­u­lar lib­er­als were the fringe, and pol­i­tics sim­ply caught up with so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
shelf.why: The con­ver­sa­tional com­pan­ion to Akshaya Mukul’s book on how the Gita Press, through cul­ture and re­li­gion, fed mod­ern po­lit­i­cal Hinduism.

shelf.title: The Lost Decade
shelf.creator: Puja Mehra
shelf.why: Puja Mehra’s ac­count of how India’s growth stalled after 2008, through de­ci­sions like ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion and the reshuf­fle that made Pranab Mukherjee fi­nance min­is­ter.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

laughs.text: On the Finnish Navy board­ing the Chinese tanker, Amit imag­ines the cap­tain ask­ing ‘Who are you and what do you want?’ and get­ting the reply ‘We are Finnish, you are fin­ished.’ Ajay help­fully notes that his own ver­sion of the punch­line was ‘and you are fin­ished.’ Amit protests: ‘Always elab­o­rat­ing on jokes... This man, I gotta tell you, freak­ing an­a­lyze the jokes... Can you im­prove the copy­writ­ing?’

After the AstraZeneca story, Amit tells Ajay that with­out the vac­cine ‘You could have been talk­ing to an empty chair. With sad­ness in your eyes.’ Ajay: ‘There would have been no Everything is Everything... Everything is noth­ing.’

Amit’s sign-off: the episode was ‘a primer, a wake up call, and a con­fes­sion,’ be­cause Ajay has been wag­ing hy­brid war­fare on him with fruit, biryani and sweets. ‘You’re killing me softly with your sugar.’ Now wise to the tac­tic, Amit vows to re­sist, though Ajay ‘may give me cof­fee and cheese.’
‘Uber for artillery’: Amit’s name for the bot­tom-up way Ukrainian forces or­gan­ise ar­tillery and am­mu­ni­tion, along­side drones strik­ing trenches far be­hind the front lines.

‘It is Swachh Bharat all over again’: Ajay on bu­reau­cra­cies where fake num­bers flow up­ward until lead­ers be­lieve them, as in Saddam’s Iraq. ‘Because a doc­u­ment says we built so many toi­lets, it doesn’t mean you should start cheer­ing.’
